dependent-types.title: What are dependent types?
dependent-types.intro: Types can describe facts about values. Start with a list-length example, then watch Osprey check an actual identity proof.
dependent-types.detail: The length-indexed list is a conceptual introduction, not a shipped Osprey API. Ordinary Osprey programs retain Hindley-Milner type inference; dependent proof terms belong to a separate checking discipline.

osprey-proof-kernel.title: How Osprey checks a proof
osprey-proof-kernel.intro: Follow a statement and its evidence through the proof kernel written in Osprey.
osprey-proof-kernel.detail: The kernel infers a proof term's type and compares it with the claimed statement. The recorded runs show both acceptance and deliberate rejection. This is a check of the supplied statement and proof, not automatic verification of an entire application.

proof-workbench.title: Use the Proof Workbench
proof-workbench.intro: Write a small argument, inspect hypotheses and goals, and complete a guided exercise in the real Workbench.
proof-workbench.detail: A Checked verdict comes from the shared Osprey kernel. A draft can still contain open goals, and unsupported or mismatched steps must be refused. The optional generated source is a separate view; its presence alone does not establish a proof.

mathlib-bridge.title: The Mathlib port is underway
mathlib-bridge.intro: See actual imported mathematical proofs being checked by Osprey, with each theorem's assumptions made visible.
mathlib-bridge.detail: The films record ten selected supporting lemmas. The current public corpus has twelve; the progress guide records the newer checkpoint separately. These are checked exports from Lean developments, not a completed port of Mathlib or the headline research theorems.

proofs-that-say-no.title: A proof checker must say no
proofs-that-say-no.intro: Compare a valid proof with deliberately corrupted evidence and a false replacement statement.
proofs-that-say-no.detail: A trustworthy check needs negative controls. Acceptance must disappear when the evidence or statement changes; a parser error or missing dependency is not a substitute for a kernel type-mismatch rejection.

navier-stokes-proof.title: Navier-Stokes: computation and proof
navier-stokes-proof.intro: Meet the fluid equations in words, see them in the Workbench, then compare a computed flow with a logical proof exercise.
navier-stokes-proof.detail: The periodic two-dimensional Taylor-Green flow is a numerical example with measured residuals. The Workbench exercise proves a propositional implication under explicit premises. Neither establishes a formal proof of the Navier-Stokes equations or the three-dimensional regularity problem. The recorded computation and residual checker are production assets in the separate TikTok repository; the Osprey source link below is the Workbench lesson.
